# Day 2 — Consolidation {#sec-day2-consolidation}

**20 minutes · plenary**

## Say it in one sentence

A colleague sends you a model fitted to `data/diabetes.csv` and a test MAE.
Without notes, write the single sentence you would send back. It must name one
property of the data that affects whether the number means anything, and one
thing you want to see before believing it.

A sentence that meets the bar:

> More than half the insulin values and a third of the skin-folds in that file
> are zeros standing in for missing measurements, so before I can read your MAE
> I need to know what you imputed them with and whether the imputer was fitted
> on the training rows alone.

## Self-assessment

Tick honestly. Anything unticked is what to review before Day 3.

- [ ] I can find values that are valid to the software and impossible in a patient, and say what fraction of a column they are.
- [ ] I can state what treating those values as missing did to two specific correlations, and in which direction.
- [ ] I can describe a missingness pattern well enough to argue about how it arose.
- [ ] I can impute a column and name two properties of the data I changed by doing it.
- [ ] I can say which of min-max, z-score and log changes the shape of a distribution.
- [ ] I can separate preprocessing steps that are fitted to data from those that are not.
- [ ] I can explain why scaling before the split cost nothing here, and why that is not a reason to do it.
- [ ] I can build a workflow or a `Pipeline` that makes the leak-free order the only available order.

## Five questions

Answer in a sentence each. These are the form the written assessment takes.

1. A column of blood pressures contains 35 zeros. A colleague says "they are
   only 5% of the data, so it will not matter". Give the two separate reasons
   that might be wrong.
2. You impute a variable with its median and the standard deviation falls by
   5%. Is that a problem with the median, with the imputation, or with
   something else?
3. Every predictor in a file has exactly 20 missing values. What do you
   conclude, and what would you have concluded if the counts had been 17, 24,
   19 and 31?
4. Standardising before the split made no difference to the test MAE at all.
   Explain why, and give one model for which the same leak would have made a
   difference.
5. A model's test MAE improves after you switch from mean imputation to a
   regression-based imputer fitted on the whole dataset. What are the two
   possible explanations, and which single piece of code would tell you which
   it is?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) First, 5% of rows is not 5% of the analysis: those zeros are
not dropped, they are averaged in, so they bias the mean and attenuate or
inflate every correlation involving the column. Second, missingness is almost
never random, so the 35 patients are probably not like the other 733 — the
question is who they are, not how many. (2) With the imputation. Replacing
values with the centre of the distribution necessarily reduces the spread; the
median is not at fault and neither is the data. It is the price of
single-value imputation, and the fix is multiple imputation or an honest
statement in the methods. (3) Exactly 20 in every column means the missingness
was injected by a script, so the file teaches mechanics and not diagnosis.
Ragged counts would have suggested a real process, at which point the next
question is whether the columns go missing together. (4) Ordinary least squares
is equivariant under affine rescaling of its predictors: every coefficient
absorbs the change and the fitted values are identical. Ridge, lasso, k-nearest
neighbours or anything else whose objective depends on the scale of the
coefficients or the distances would have been affected. (5) Either the better
imputer genuinely helps, or it leaked — the imputation model was allowed to see
the outcome, or the test rows, or both. Refit the imputer on the training rows
with the outcome column excluded; if the improvement survives, it was real.

**Rubric** (if the day is assessed, 20 marks):

| | Marks |
|---|---|
| Zero audit complete, with the impossible zeros correctly distinguished from the legitimate ones | 4 |
| Correlation recomputed with zeros as missing, and at least one entry named as changed, with direction | 3 |
| Missingness pattern described, and a reasoned conclusion about how it arose | 3 |
| Imputation performed, with one named consequence measured rather than asserted | 3 |
| Leaking and leak-free pipelines both built, with both MAEs reported | 4 |
| One sentence stating what the comparison does and does not show | 3 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[80,20]"}

Mark the reasoning, not the verdict. A student who concludes that scaling
leakage is harmless *and shows the identity that makes it harmless here* has
understood more than one who recites the rule and cannot say when it bites.

**If the cohort is ahead**, set Stretch 3 of @sec-leakage — selection leakage
with noise predictors — as a group exercise and run it from the front. It is
the most dramatic of the three and the hardest to spot in a colleague's code.
:::
:::

## What carries into Day 3

Three loose ends, each of which opens the next session.

1. **Everything was measured with one model.** Linear regression was a
   measuring instrument today, not a choice. Day 3 asks where its coefficients
   come from, what loss it is minimising, and why that loss and not another.
2. **The split is still a single split.** Every number in the scoreboard rests
   on one arbitrary 80/20 partition of 755 patients. Resampling is what turns
   those numbers into estimates with a spread, and your preprocessing has to
   live inside the resampling loop — which is why it had to come first.
3. **"Better MAE" was never defined.** The scoreboard ranked five pipelines by
   a metric nobody justified, on an outcome whose units carry clinical meaning.
   Day 5 takes metrics apart; Day 3 starts by taking the loss apart.

## Further reading

TRIPOD+AI, the reporting standard for clinical prediction models, asks you to
state how missing data were handled and how predictors were preprocessed, and
to do so in enough detail that a reader could repeat it [@collins2024]. Read
those items with today in mind: they exist because the papers in Wynants and
colleagues' appraisal of covid-19 prediction models were, in large part, not
reproducible on exactly those points [@wynants2020].
